Model providers sell several tiers at very different prices,
and a working session does not need the strongest tier for every step.
The cost lever that field reports name most often is to split the work by tier:

- **Plan with the strongest model you can afford.**
  Architecture, task breakdown, and the decisions that are expensive to reverse
  benefit most from the extra reasoning,
  and they are a small share of the tokens a project spends.
- **Implement with cheaper models.**
  Well-specified edits, boilerplate, tests, and documentation are where the token volume goes,
  and a mid-tier or small model handles them once the plan is explicit.
- **Constrain the scope deliberately.**
  Keep the vision to what can realistically ship,
  so the result is a working product rather than a promise,
  and iterate from there.

The same field report behind the framing in @sec-ai-relative-advantages,
a four-month browser-game build by a non-programmer
(r/ClaudeCode, 2026-08-22, "Vibe coded this game in four months"),
put its total spend at roughly $200 over four months on subscriptions taken out for the project,
on top of a shared general-purpose subscription,
with planning on the strongest model and implementation on cheaper ones as the main saving.

Two neighboring sections cover the vendor-specific and the model-specific halves of this:
@sec-ai-gemini-spend-management is about one provider's API spend,
and @sec-ai-small-local-models is about running cheap or local models at all.
This section is the routing rule between tiers,
which is also stated for agents in the lab's machine-facing configuration,
[`Morrison-Lab/ai-config`](https://github.com/Morrison-Lab/ai-config).
